chapterTitle: Common Troubleshooting Scenarios: Network Setup and Connectivity
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute live terminal troubleshooting video. Start with a 2-minute overview of a systematic troubleshooting approach. Then, for 10 minutes, demonstrate three common issues:
1.  **Docker compose failure**: Intentionally introduce a port conflict in `docker-compose.yaml`, run `docker-compose up`, show the container exiting, use `docker logs` to diagnose "port already in use", and fix it.
2.  **TLS handshake failure**: Intentionally point a `peer` CLI command's `--cafile` to an incorrect TLS CA, run the command, show the `x509` error, explain it, and fix it.
3.  **Gossip sync issue**: Briefly show `peer channel getinfo` on two peers with different block heights, then show how to check `docker logs <peer_container>` for `[gossip]` errors (e.g., "failed to connect").
Conclude with a 3-minute segment summarizing key diagnostic commands (`docker ps`, `docker logs`, `netstat`, `peer channel getinfo`) and a checklist for network setup. Interactive element: a "spot the error" challenge in a `docker-compose.yaml` snippet. Visual style: terminal demos, split-screen showing `docker-compose.yaml` and terminal, diagram overlays explaining network flow. Accessibility: captions, detailed transcript, high-contrast visuals.

screens.title: Common Troubleshooting Scenarios: Network Setup and Connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on practical, repeatable ways to diagnose and resolve the most common network and connectivity problems you will meet when standing up a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will learn to interpret container states, read container and component logs, check peer gossip and peer-to-orderer links, and isolate TLS and certificate trust failures. We emphasize a simple workflow you can use every time: confirm container health, collect targeted logs, reproduce the failed action, and verify network reachability. For example, when a peer exits immediately, the pattern is to run docker ps -a, then docker logs for that peer, check for port conflicts, permission errors, or missing environment variables, and then apply the focused fix. This chapter matters because quick diagnosis saves hours in production and prevents cascading misconfigurations. As we progress you will see concrete command examples, sample error messages like x509 certificate errors, and a hands-on activity that intentionally misconfigures a peer TLS CA so you can practice diagnosing and repairing it. By the end you will be able to reason about connectivity, certificates, and process health with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you'll have four practical troubleshooting skills that are directly applicable when setting up or maintaining a Fabric network. First, you will identify container-level startup issues using docker ps and docker logs, and interpret common messages such as port conflicts or permission denied. This matters because correct startup is the gateway to all higher-level operations. Second, you will diagnose peer-to-peer gossip and ledger synchronization failures by comparing block heights and reviewing gossip-related log entries. You'll learn how anchor peers and Docker networking impact discovery. Third, you will troubleshoot peer-to-orderer connectivity, verify orderer availability, and ensure correct TLS trust materials. This skill prevents failed transactions and stale ledgers. Fourth, you will detect and resolve CA registration and enrollment errors, understand enrollment tokens and server-side authorization errors, and fix mispointed TLS CA files. Each objective pairs a command set with a clear resolution path so you can act confidently when you see a failure. These skills reduce downtime and help you keep channels healthy and consistent across organizations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Commands
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide maps each troubleshooting skill to the commands and verification steps you'll use in practice. For container startup issues you'll rely on docker ps -a to see status and docker logs to read errors; common messages to watch for include port already in use, permission denied, or missing environment variables. For peer gossip and ledger sync problems you'll use peer channel getinfo to compare block heights and inspect peer logs for gossip module messages such as handshake failed or no active peers. For peer-to-orderer issues pair peer logs with orderer logs and use network checks such as netstat or a simple telnet to verify ports are reachable. For identity and TLS problems you will check fabric-ca-server logs and fabric-ca-client output, ensure the FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME and TLS cafile variables are correct, and confirm that the TLS root certificate referenced actually matches the orderer's CA. Practicing these exact steps will give you a reliable diagnosis path and reduce trial-and-error time during network start and maintenance.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.7 › Commands & Verification
Container startup
docker ps -a
docker logs <container_name>
# Inspect exit codes and stderr for port or permission errors
Look for: "port already in use", "permission denied", missing env vars
Peer & gossip
peer channel getinfo -c <channel>
peer channel list
netstat -tulnp  # inside peer to confirm gossip port
Compare block heights and find gossip handshake messages in logs
Orderer connectivity
docker logs <orderer>
peer channel getinfo -c <channel> --orderer localhost:7050 --tls --cafile <path>
Look for: connection refused, TLS handshake failed, orderer unavailable
CA and TLS
docker logs <fabric_ca_server>
fabric-ca-client enroll/register
# Verify FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME and TLS cafile paths
Common messages: authorization failure, x509: certificate signed by unknown authority

screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Start every troubleshooting session with a small, reliable workflow. First, confirm container and service state using docker ps -a. This tells you which containers exited, restarted, or are healthy. Second, gather focused logs with docker logs for the failing container and related components; logs often include specific error strings such as port already in use or permission denied. Third, reproduce the failure with the same command or action to capture fresh errors, like peer channel getinfo or a client invoke. Fourth, verify network and port reachability with netstat, ping, or a simple TCP check; ensure the expected gossip and orderer ports are listening and not blocked by a host firewall. Fifth, inspect TLS and certificate paths to confirm that the root CA files are correctly referenced and not expired. Finally, apply a small, reversible fix—change a compose port, correct a path, or restart a single service—and re-run verification. A common misconception is to change many variables at once; that makes root cause impossible to confirm. Always change one variable, retest, and record the outcome. This process reduces guesswork and gives you evidence for the next step.

keyIdea.title: One-step-at-a-time
keyIdea.text: Change a single thing, retest, and verify. Use logs and network checks to gather evidence before applying fixes.

content.html:
Process Flow
Repeatable troubleshooting steps
1. Confirm state
docker ps -a to find exited or restarting containers.
2. Collect logs
docker logs <name> for ERROR, FATAL, x509, or gossip messages.
3. Reproduce and verify
Run the failing command (peer channel getinfo, chaincode invoke) to capture errors in real time.
4. Network checks
Use netstat, ping, or TCP checks to confirm ports like 7051 and 7050 are reachable.
5. TLS & certs
Verify TLS root cert paths and validity; check hostname overrides if SANs differ.
Example diagnostic session
# 1. Check containers
docker ps -a
# 2. If peer exits, collect logs
docker logs peer0.org1.example.com
# 3. Reproduce the failing action
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --tls --cafile /path/to/orderer-ca.pem
# 4. Check listening ports inside peer
netstat -tulnp
Key Takeaway

Follow a consistent flow: state, logs, reproduce, network, certs. Change one item per iteration to confirm the fix.

screens.title: docker-compose setup failures
screens.narratorSegment: When docker-compose fails to start a Fabric network, the first evidence is container state. An Exited or Restarting container is a signal to run docker logs for that service. Logs frequently include clear, actionable messages. For port conflicts you will see text such as port already in use. This happens when another local process or another compose service uses the same host port; the fix is to stop the conflicting process or adjust the compose mapping. For permission denied errors the container may be unable to read crypto material or ledger volumes; check host ownership and use chmod or chown to grant the container process access. Missing environment variables show up as configuration errors; ensure variables like CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID or ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED are present in docker-compose. yaml. Incorrect volume mounts are also common: if the path is wrong the container cannot access TLS or MSP files. A misconception is to assume docker itself is broken. Most startup failures are configuration issues surfaced by logs. The concrete method is: docker ps -a, then docker logs, then inspect compose for ports, volumes, and env vars, and apply the smallest fix. After change, re-run docker-compose up for that service and re-check logs.

keyIdea.title: Read the logs first
keyIdea.text: Container logs reveal port conflicts, permission issues, and missing environment variables—fix those before restarting the whole network.

content.html:
Definition
docker-compose setup failures
Containers failing to start commonly indicate port conflicts, file permission problems, missing environment variables, or incorrect volume mounts.
# Inspect container states
docker ps -a
# Check logs for a stopped container
docker logs peer0.org1.example.com
# Example log snippets you might see
# "port already in use"
# "permission denied" when accessing /var/hyperledger/production
# "missing environment variable: CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID"
Concrete example & fix
If logs show "port already in use" for 7050, identify the conflicting process and free the port or remap the Fabric service to another host port. If logs show permission denied for crypto material, correct owner and mode.
# Stop conflicting process (example)
sudo lsof -i :7050
sudo kill <pid>
# Fix permissions
sudo chown -R $(id -u):$(id -g) ./organizations
sudo chmod -R 0755 ./organizations
Common mistake

Changing many settings at once. Change one item, restart, and confirm the error disappears before proceeding.

screens.title: Peer-to-peer (gossip) connectivity issues
screens.narratorSegment: Peer-to-peer connectivity in Fabric relies on the gossip protocol to disseminate blocks and state. When gossip fails, peers will show different block heights and may not list the same channels. One clear diagnostic is peer channel getinfo: compare block heights across peers to confirm if a peer is behind. The peer logs will often include [gossip] module messages such as failed to connect to peer, handshake failed, or no active peers. Use docker logs for the peer container to capture these messages. Inside the peer container use netstat -tulnp to confirm that the gossip port (commonly 7051) is listening and that outbound connections are being attempted. Anchor peers are crucial for discovery: if anchor peers are missing or misconfigured the initial peer discovery may fail and leave peers isolated. A common network misstep is placing peers on different Docker networks with no cross-host routing; ensure peers share a reachable network or enable cross-host connectivity. Also check TLS: gossip connections may require mutual TLS, so the root CA files must be trusted by peers. A common misconception is to blame chaincode; often ledger lag is a connectivity or discovery problem. The takeaway is to compare block heights, read gossip errors, and verify port reachability and anchor peer definitions before changing higher-level config.

keyIdea.title: Gossip needs reachability and anchors
keyIdea.text: If peers disagree on block height, check gossip logs, ports, Docker networks, and anchor peer definitions to restore discovery and sync.

content.html:
Definition
Peer-to-peer (gossip) connectivity
Gossip propagates blocks and state. Failures cause peers to diverge in block height or miss channels.
# Compare heights
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel
# Check peer logs for gossip errors
docker logs peer0.org1.example.com | grep gossip
# Inside container: is gossip port listening?
netstat -tulnp
Resolution checklist
  • Confirm gossip ports are listening and accessible.
  • Verify anchor peers are defined and present in channel config.
  • Ensure peers are on the same Docker network or routed across hosts.
  • Check TLS root CAs for gossip trust relationships.
Key Takeaway

Ledger divergence is usually a connectivity or discovery issue. Start with block height comparison and gossip logs, then confirm network reachability and anchor peers.

screens.title: Anchor peers and network configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Anchor peers are special because they are the initial discovery points other organizations use to find peers on a channel. Unlike regular peers, anchor peers are included in the channel configuration so peers can bootstrap discovery across org boundaries. When anchor peers are misconfigured or omitted, peers can remain isolated inside their organization and fail to discover peers in other orgs, which causes incomplete block propagation. To diagnose anchor-related issues, inspect the channel configuration to ensure anchor peer entries exist for each organization. A concrete test is to compare peer channel list outputs on different peers; if channels are missing on one peer, it may not have discovered peers in other orgs. Another common error is using the wrong host or port for anchor peers in the configuration—this causes attempted connections to fail. A misconception is that any running peer will automatically discover all others; discovery depends on anchor entries and network reachability. The recommended resolution is to update the channel config with correct anchor peer endpoints and then have peers re-discover through standard gossip initiation. This restores cross-organization propagation without changing endorsement or ACL policies.

keyIdea.title: Anchors enable cross-org discovery
keyIdea.text: Ensure anchor peers are defined and reachable; discovery will fail if anchor endpoints are incorrect or unreachable.

content.html:
Comparison
Anchor peer vs Regular peer
Anchor peer
Listed in channel config, used for cross-org discovery, must be reachable by other orgs.
Regular peer
Participates in gossip and endorses transactions but is not advertised for discovery unless configured.
Concrete checks
  • Inspect channel config for anchor entries per org.
  • Confirm host and port in anchor entry are reachable from other peers.
  • After updating anchors, allow gossip time to reseed and synchronize ledgers.
Key Takeaway

Anchor peers are a discovery contract. Correct anchor entries and reachable endpoints are necessary for peers to find each other across organizations.

screens.title: Peer-to-orderer connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Peers must be able to reach orderers to submit proposals for ordering and to receive blocks. When transactions are not being ordered or block heights do not progress, start by checking both peer and orderer container logs. Peer logs may show connection refused or TLS handshake failed; orderer logs may indicate client connection errors. Use peer channel getinfo to confirm whether the peer’s block height is increasing. If the orderer container is not healthy, ensure it is running and listening on the expected port. A useful network test is a TCP connection to the orderer port from the peer container context; this demonstrates basic reachability. TLS misconfiguration is a frequent culprit: verify the peer's CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE points to the orderer's TLS CA, and ensure the orderer's ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ROOTCAS trusts the peer's CA when mutual TLS is used. Hostname mismatches require the TLSHostnameOverride to align the presented certificate SAN with the connection hostname. A misconception is that orderer failures are always due to ordering service mode; often the peer simply cannot reach or trust the orderer. Fixes include correcting cafile paths, opening ports, or updating hostname overrides, then retrying peer channel joins or getinfo until block heights advance.

keyIdea.title: Orderer reachability + trust
keyIdea.text: Ensure orderers are healthy and reachable, and verify TLS root CA paths so peers can submit proposals and receive blocks.

content.html:
Core Concept
Peer-to-orderer connectivity
Ordering requires both reachability and correct TLS trust between peers and orderers.
# Check peer side
docker logs peer0.org1.example.com | tail -n 200
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --tls --cafile /path/to/orderer-ca.pem
# Check orderer side
docker logs orderer.example.com
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Confirm orderer is running and listening on its port.
  2. From the peer context, test TCP reachability to the orderer.
  3. Validate CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE points to the orderer's TLS CA.
  4. Apply TLSHostnameOverride if SAN mismatches occur.
Key Takeaway

Ordering problems are usually reachability or TLS trust issues. Confirm both sides see each other and trust the same root CAs.

screens.title: CA registration and enrollment failures
screens.narratorSegment: Identity management relies on the Fabric CA. When fabric-ca-client register or enroll fails, the root cause is often visible in the CA server logs. Authorization failures or invalid token errors indicate the enrolling identity lacks permission to register new users; verify that the admin identity used for registration has proper privileges recorded in the CA registry. Identity already exists is self-explanatory and may require using a different name or cleaning the CA's registry for development. Certificate request failed points to issues in CSR generation or unsupported attributes. On the client side make sure FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME points to the appropriate MSP directory and that FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_TLS_CERTFILES references the CA's TLS certificate so the client trusts the server. A common mistake is assuming the CA is unreachable; often the CA is running but the enrollment credentials or TLS paths are incorrect. The resolution path is: check CA server logs, confirm the admin identity and its permissions, verify client environment variables and TLS cert paths, and reattempt registration or enrollment. If TLS is involved, ensure cafiles match the CA's TLS root certificate to avoid handshake errors.

keyIdea.title: CA errors are either auth or TLS
keyIdea.text: Differentiate authorization failures from TLS/csr problems by inspecting both server logs and the client environment settings.

content.html:
Definition
CA registration & enrollment failures
Caused by authorization, existing identities, CSR problems, or mispointed TLS/identity paths.
# Server logs
docker logs fabric-ca-server
# Client commands
fabric-ca-client register --id.name user1 --id.secret userpw
fabric-ca-client enroll -u https://user1:userpw@ca.example.com:7054
Checks and fixes
  • Confirm CA server is reachable and logs show the request.
  • Verify enrollment credentials and admin permissions in the CA registry.
  • Ensure FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME and FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_TLS_CERTFILES are correct.
  • For CSR or cert expiration, regenerate crypto material if necessary.
Common mistake

Using a user identity instead of an admin for registration. Registration requires an identity with registry permissions.

screens.title: TLS handshake failures and certificate issues
screens.narratorSegment: TLS handshake failures are among the most common and perplexing connectivity problems. They typically appear as x509: certificate signed by unknown authority, bad certificate, or handshake failed in container logs. The diagnosis begins with reading the component logs to capture the exact x509 message and then validating that the TLS root CA file referenced by environment variables like CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE or ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ROOTCAS actually contains the correct CA certificate for the other component. Mutual TLS requires both sides to trust each other's CA. Also confirm certificate validity dates to rule out expiration. Hostname mismatches are another frequent cause: if the certificate's SAN does not match the host you connect to, use TLSHostnameOverride to align the connection name with the certificate. A common remediation path is to correct cafile environment variables to point to the correct root CA for the other component, or regenerate crypto material for development if certificates appear corrupted or expired. Remember that copying the wrong CA file between orgs or pointing to an org's peer TLS CA when connecting to the orderer will cause trust failures. Validate with a successful peer channel getinfo using the corrected cafile, and the x509 errors should disappear.

narration.text: TLS handshake failures are among the most common and perplexing connectivity problems. They typically appear as x509: certificate signed by unknown authority, bad certificate, or handshake failed in container logs. The diagnosis begins with reading the component logs to capture the exact x509 message and then validating that the TLS root CA file referenced by environment variables like CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE or ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ROOTCAS actually contains the correct CA certificate for the other component. Mutual TLS requires both sides to trust each other's CA. Also confirm certificate validity dates to rule out expiration. Hostname mismatches are another frequent cause: if the certificate's SAN does not match the host you connect to, use TLSHostnameOverride to align the connection name with the certificate. A common remediation path is to correct cafile environment variables to point to the correct root CA for the other component, or regenerate crypto material for development if certificates appear corrupted or expired. Remember that copying the wrong CA file between orgs or pointing to an org's peer TLS CA when connecting to the orderer will cause trust failures. Validate with a successful peer channel getinfo using the corrected cafile, and the x509 errors should disappear.

Definition
TLS handshake failures
Errors like x509: certificate signed by unknown authority indicate that the client does not trust the server's TLS CA.
# Look for x509 errors

# Confirm CAFILE paths used when connecting
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --tls --cafile /path/to/orderer-ca.pem
Fix checklist
  • Confirm cafile paths point to the orderer's TLS CA when contacting the orderer.
  • Ensure both sides trust each other's root CAs for mutual TLS.
  • Check certificate validity and regenerate crypto in development if corrupted or expired.
  • Use TLSHostnameOverride when hostname and SAN differ.
Common mistake

Pointing the peer's cafile to the wrong org's TLS CA. The cafile must match the server you are connecting to.

screens.title: Activity: Introduce and fix a TLS misconfiguration
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through intentionally misconfiguring the orderer's cafile to provoke a TLS handshake failure, then diagnosing and fixing it. Start a clean test-network and confirm initial connectivity by running peer channel getinfo which should succeed. Next, change the ORDERER_CA environment variable to point to the wrong certificate—an Org1 peer TLS CA instead of the orderer's TLS CA. Re-run the peer channel getinfo command and observe the errors: you may see connection failed messages or x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. Use docker logs on the peer to capture the exact error text and verify it references x509. Your diagnosis is that the client cafile does not match the orderer's CA, so the peer cannot validate the orderer's certificate. To fix it, reset ORDERER_CA to the correct path for the orderer TLS CA and re-run the peer channel getinfo command. Confirm the command now returns block height information. This activity reinforces reading the error text, tracing environment variables to actual certificate files, and validating that the cafile matches the server CA, which are the exact steps you will use in production to repair TLS trust issues.

Activity
Troubleshoot a TLS connectivity issue
Follow these steps exactly to exercise diagnosis and fix procedures.
# 1. Start a clean network
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -ca

# 2. Verify connectivity
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls --cafile $ORDERER_CA

# 3. Introduce error (intentional)
export ORDERER_CA=./organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls --cafile $ORDERER_CA
Diagnose and resolve
You should see x509 errors in the peer output. Fix by resetting ORDERER_CA to the orderer's TLS CA and re-run the command.
export ORDERER_CA=./organizations/ordererOrganizations/example.com/orderers/orderer.example.com/msp/tlscacerts/tlsca.example.com-cert.pem
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel --orderer localhost:7050 --ordererTLSHostnameOverride orderer.example.com --tls --cafile $ORDERER_CA
Key Takeaway

Practice reproducing the error, locate the incorrect cafile, and restore the correct TLS CA to confirm the network is healthy again.

screens.title: Common resource and permission problems
screens.narratorSegment: Resource and permission problems often masquerade as general startup failures. For example, an Exited (137) container status plus messages about memory cgroup out of memory points to the container being killed due to memory pressure. The likely cause is insufficient memory allocated to Docker or the container itself. Fixes include increasing Docker daemon memory on Docker Desktop, setting mem_limit or memswap_limit in docker-compose. yaml for the peer service, or optimizing chaincode to reduce memory usage. Another frequent class of errors is file permission when containers cannot read crypto material mounted from the host. The logs show permission denied when accessing /var/hyperledger or tls files. Resolve these by chowning the directories to the host UID used by the container process and applying restrictive but correct modes with chmod. A common misconception is to restart containers without addressing the underlying resource limits; the container will be killed again if limits remain too low. After applying resource increases or permission fixes, restart the affected container and monitor docker logs to confirm the problem is resolved. This focused approach turns intermittent exits into a stable, repeatable environment.

keyIdea.title: Match resources to workload
keyIdea.text: Exited (137) usually means the process was OOM-killed. Increase daemon or container memory or optimize workloads, and fix file ownership for mounted volumes.

content.html:
Scenario
Memory and permission issues
Exited (137) plus memory cgroup messages indicate an out-of-memory kill. Permission denied messages point to host volume ownership problems.
# Example: increase memory limits in docker-compose
services:
  peer0.org1.example.com:
    mem_limit: 2g
    memswap_limit: 2g

# Fix permissions
sudo chown -R $(id -u):$(id -g) ./organizations
sudo chmod -R 0755 ./organizations
Checks and confirmation
  • Inspect docker logs for OOM messages.
  • Raise Docker daemon memory for local environments.
  • Set mem_limit in compose for persistent fixes.
  • Adjust file ownership for mounted crypto material.
Key Takeaway

Resource constraints and file ownership are common causes of repeated container exits. Fix limits and permissions, then restart and verify with logs.

screens.title: Diagnosing ACL and authorization errors
screens.narratorSegment: Access control and ACL errors are distinct from network or TLS problems and require configuration changes to policies. An error like access denied: creator org is not authorized to invoke indicates the client identity does not satisfy the channel ACL for the requested action. The first step is to recognize this is an authorization issue rather than a connectivity or TLS failure. Inspect the exact error which usually names the ACL or action, such as _lifecycle/ChaincodeInstantiate. Then review the channel configuration's ACLs section to see which identities or roles are permitted. The fix is either to use an authorized identity (for example an admin from a permitted org) or to update the ACL policy to include the required organization or role if that is appropriate. Updating ACLs requires constructing and submitting a channel configuration update, which should be done carefully and with governance in mind. A common misconception is to loosen ACLs broadly; prefer granting the minimum required permissions and using the correct admin identity for privileged operations. This understanding prevents accidental privilege escalation and ensures chaincode lifecycle operations are conducted by authorized parties only.

content.html:
Comparison
Authorization vs Connectivity
Authorization errors name the policy preventing an action. Connectivity errors prevent reaching the service; they look like connection refused or x509 errors.
# Example error
access denied: channel [mychannel] creator org [Org1MSP] is not authorized to invoke [_lifecycle/ChaincodeInstantiate]

# Fix path options
# 1. Use an authorized admin identity
# 2. Update ACLs in channel config (with governance steps)
Resolution guidance
  • Confirm the identity used has the required role (admin vs user).
  • Inspect the channel ACLs section to see authorized roles.
  • If policy change is needed, prepare a channel config update with proper signatures.
Assessment idea

Given an access denied error, identify whether to change the identity or the ACL. Document the governance steps required for a config update.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on practical, repeatable ways to diagnose and resolve the most common network and connectivity problems you will meet when standing up a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will learn to interpret container states, read container and component logs, check peer gossip and peer-to-orderer links, and isolate TLS and certificate trust failures. We emphasize a simple workflow you can use every time: confirm container health, collect targeted logs, reproduce the failed action, and verify network reachability. For example, when a peer exits immediately, the pattern is to run docker ps -a, then docker logs for that peer, check for port conflicts, permission errors, or missing environment variables, and then apply the focused fix. This chapter matters because quick diagnosis saves hours in production and prevents cascading misconfigurations. As we progress you will see concrete command examples, sample error messages like x509 certificate errors, and a hands-on activity that intentionally misconfigures a peer TLS CA so you can practice diagnosing and repairing it. By the end you will be able to reason about connectivity, certificates, and process health with confidence.

By the end of this chapter you'll have four practical troubleshooting skills that are directly applicable when setting up or maintaining a Fabric network. First, you will identify container-level startup issues using docker ps and docker logs, and interpret common messages such as port conflicts or permission denied. This matters because correct startup is the gateway to all higher-level operations. Second, you will diagnose peer-to-peer gossip and ledger synchronization failures by comparing block heights and reviewing gossip-related log entries. You'll learn how anchor peers and Docker networking impact discovery. Third, you will troubleshoot peer-to-orderer connectivity, verify orderer availability, and ensure correct TLS trust materials. This skill prevents failed transactions and stale ledgers. Fourth, you will detect and resolve CA registration and enrollment errors, understand enrollment tokens and server-side authorization errors, and fix mispointed TLS CA files. Each objective pairs a command set with a clear resolution path so you can act confidently when you see a failure. These skills reduce downtime and help you keep channels healthy and consistent across organizations.

This second objectives slide maps each troubleshooting skill to the commands and verification steps you'll use in practice. For container startup issues you'll rely on docker ps -a to see status and docker logs to read errors; common messages to watch for include port already in use, permission denied, or missing environment variables. For peer gossip and ledger sync problems you'll use peer channel getinfo to compare block heights and inspect peer logs for gossip module messages such as handshake failed or no active peers. For peer-to-orderer issues pair peer logs with orderer logs and use network checks such as netstat or a simple telnet to verify ports are reachable. For identity and TLS problems you will check fabric-ca-server logs and fabric-ca-client output, ensure the FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME and TLS cafile variables are correct, and confirm that the TLS root certificate referenced actually matches the orderer's CA. Practicing these exact steps will give you a reliable diagnosis path and reduce trial-and-error time during network start and maintenance.

Start every troubleshooting session with a small, reliable workflow. First, confirm container and service state using docker ps -a. This tells you which containers exited, restarted, or are healthy. Second, gather focused logs with docker logs for the failing container and related components; logs often include specific error strings such as port already in use or permission denied. Third, reproduce the failure with the same command or action to capture fresh errors, like peer channel getinfo or a client invoke. Fourth, verify network and port reachability with netstat, ping, or a simple TCP check; ensure the expected gossip and orderer ports are listening and not blocked by a host firewall. Fifth, inspect TLS and certificate paths to confirm that the root CA files are correctly referenced and not expired. Finally, apply a small, reversible fix—change a compose port, correct a path, or restart a single service—and re-run verification. A common misconception is to change many variables at once; that makes root cause impossible to confirm. Always change one variable, retest, and record the outcome. This process reduces guesswork and gives you evidence for the next step.

When docker-compose fails to start a Fabric network, the first evidence is container state. An Exited or Restarting container is a signal to run docker logs for that service. Logs frequently include clear, actionable messages. For port conflicts you will see text such as port already in use. This happens when another local process or another compose service uses the same host port; the fix is to stop the conflicting process or adjust the compose mapping. For permission denied errors the container may be unable to read crypto material or ledger volumes; check host ownership and use chmod or chown to grant the container process access. Missing environment variables show up as configuration errors; ensure variables like CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID or ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED are present in docker-compose. yaml. Incorrect volume mounts are also common: if the path is wrong the container cannot access TLS or MSP files. A misconception is to assume docker itself is broken. Most startup failures are configuration issues surfaced by logs. The concrete method is: docker ps -a, then docker logs, then inspect compose for ports, volumes, and env vars, and apply the smallest fix. After change, re-run docker-compose up for that service and re-check logs.

Peer-to-peer connectivity in Fabric relies on the gossip protocol to disseminate blocks and state. When gossip fails, peers will show different block heights and may not list the same channels. One clear diagnostic is peer channel getinfo: compare block heights across peers to confirm if a peer is behind. The peer logs will often include [gossip] module messages such as failed to connect to peer, handshake failed, or no active peers. Use docker logs for the peer container to capture these messages. Inside the peer container use netstat -tulnp to confirm that the gossip port (commonly 7051) is listening and that outbound connections are being attempted. Anchor peers are crucial for discovery: if anchor peers are missing or misconfigured the initial peer discovery may fail and leave peers isolated. A common network misstep is placing peers on different Docker networks with no cross-host routing; ensure peers share a reachable network or enable cross-host connectivity. Also check TLS: gossip connections may require mutual TLS, so the root CA files must be trusted by peers. A common misconception is to blame chaincode; often ledger lag is a connectivity or discovery problem. The takeaway is to compare block heights, read gossip errors, and verify port reachability and anchor peer definitions before changing higher-level config.

Anchor peers are special because they are the initial discovery points other organizations use to find peers on a channel. Unlike regular peers, anchor peers are included in the channel configuration so peers can bootstrap discovery across org boundaries. When anchor peers are misconfigured or omitted, peers can remain isolated inside their organization and fail to discover peers in other orgs, which causes incomplete block propagation. To diagnose anchor-related issues, inspect the channel configuration to ensure anchor peer entries exist for each organization. A concrete test is to compare peer channel list outputs on different peers; if channels are missing on one peer, it may not have discovered peers in other orgs. Another common error is using the wrong host or port for anchor peers in the configuration—this causes attempted connections to fail. A misconception is that any running peer will automatically discover all others; discovery depends on anchor entries and network reachability. The recommended resolution is to update the channel config with correct anchor peer endpoints and then have peers re-discover through standard gossip initiation. This restores cross-organization propagation without changing endorsement or ACL policies.

Peers must be able to reach orderers to submit proposals for ordering and to receive blocks. When transactions are not being ordered or block heights do not progress, start by checking both peer and orderer container logs. Peer logs may show connection refused or TLS handshake failed; orderer logs may indicate client connection errors. Use peer channel getinfo to confirm whether the peer’s block height is increasing. If the orderer container is not healthy, ensure it is running and listening on the expected port. A useful network test is a TCP connection to the orderer port from the peer container context; this demonstrates basic reachability. TLS misconfiguration is a frequent culprit: verify the peer's CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE points to the orderer's TLS CA, and ensure the orderer's ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ROOTCAS trusts the peer's CA when mutual TLS is used. Hostname mismatches require the TLSHostnameOverride to align the presented certificate SAN with the connection hostname. A misconception is that orderer failures are always due to ordering service mode; often the peer simply cannot reach or trust the orderer. Fixes include correcting cafile paths, opening ports, or updating hostname overrides, then retrying peer channel joins or getinfo until block heights advance.

Identity management relies on the Fabric CA. When fabric-ca-client register or enroll fails, the root cause is often visible in the CA server logs. Authorization failures or invalid token errors indicate the enrolling identity lacks permission to register new users; verify that the admin identity used for registration has proper privileges recorded in the CA registry. Identity already exists is self-explanatory and may require using a different name or cleaning the CA's registry for development. Certificate request failed points to issues in CSR generation or unsupported attributes. On the client side make sure FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME points to the appropriate MSP directory and that FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_TLS_CERTFILES references the CA's TLS certificate so the client trusts the server. A common mistake is assuming the CA is unreachable; often the CA is running but the enrollment credentials or TLS paths are incorrect. The resolution path is: check CA server logs, confirm the admin identity and its permissions, verify client environment variables and TLS cert paths, and reattempt registration or enrollment. If TLS is involved, ensure cafiles match the CA's TLS root certificate to avoid handshake errors.

Rule two: verify network and port reachability for gossip and orderer communication; many sync issues are caused by unreachable ports or misconfigured Docker networks. Rule three: treat TLS errors as trust problems; ensure cafile paths match the server CA, check for expired certs, and use hostname overrides when SANs require them.
